description: Adversary Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: 6 years of Adversary Village Keeping up with the adversaries and why it takes a village
talks.teaser: Looks back at six years of Adversary Village, from early debates over emulation versus simulation to how AI fits into adversary testing.
talks.summary:
This panel marks the sixth year of Adversary Village, a DEF CON space for people who study and test adversary tradecraft. The organizers recall the village's cramped first meeting, when fire marshals had to clear an overfilled room, and explain how submissions are reviewed so that talks stay focused on adversary behavior instead of overlapping with other villages.

A recurring theme is the difference between simulation and emulation. One panelist describes simulation as reproducing the indicators and commands seen in a real campaign, which pays off early but goes stale quickly. Emulation instead models how a particular threat would act against a specific organization, using knowledge of its motives, business units and weak points. The group argues that the industry still lacks clarity on these terms, and that practitioners need to explain the distinction to executives who decide how testing is funded.

On AI, the speakers see generative models as a multiplier that amplifies the skill of whoever directs them. They caution that using models to choose the right next step after initial access is hard, that generated attack code often repeats the same flaws, and that command and control and post-compromise techniques have changed little. They close by asking for work that goes beyond rehashing known techniques, including honest accounts of what did not work, and invite attendees to the village's hands-on labs and full-scope CTF.

talks.title: Beyond the Hype The Real Role of Red Teams in an AI World
talks.teaser: Explains how red teams choose adversaries to emulate, drive defensive change through storytelling, and adapt their work to AI-driven attackers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with adversary simulation, the core work of red teams. Because the threat landscape is too large to cover, teams must pick which threat actors to emulate, and the speakers describe a trade-off: higher fidelity to a known actor costs more time and effort, while emulating several actors at once sacrifices accuracy. They suggest grounding these choices in threat intelligence and treating costly capabilities, such as developing zero-day exploits, as an ongoing research effort rather than a single operation.

Next, they argue that red teams drive change by telling a clear story tied to business impact and by acting as a sparring partner for defenders. Sharing the full activity log, including failed attempts, helps blue teams see where to add or fix detection signals. Engagements can also surface known unknowns, risks people suspect but cannot act on, including the watermelon problem where indicators look green but the system is red.

On AI, the speakers say attackers gain scale, speed and tireless patience, so defenders need faster benchmarking, tests of existing controls against AI-driven intrusion, and new controls such as honey tokens. Mapping exercises into attack graphs can reveal choke points worth investing in, and AI agents themselves introduce prompt-injection risk. Their takeaway is that AI changes attackers, defenders and red teams alike, and red teams should use it to emulate and study threats.

talks.title: Emulating the Identity First Threat Actor - Automated Playbooks for IdP Hijacking
talks.teaser: Shows how to emulate identity-first intrusions across Active Directory, Entra ID and cloud control planes, and score detection coverage with repeatable playbooks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shift in how intrusions begin: attackers often log in with valid identities instead of deploying malware, so endpoint-focused emulation misses much of the activity. The speakers describe an identity-first kill chain with six phases, running from initial access and persistence through discovery, privilege escalation and trust manipulation, ending with pivots into SaaS or cloud. Each step is written as a detection contract that names the expected identity-provider or cloud log, a detection hypothesis, typical failure points, and the evidence that shows a control worked.

The middle section covers scoring. Playbooks are rated on a five-level scale, from blind (no telemetry) through event-only and huntable, up to level three, where an alert fires on time with usable fidelity. Three examples were walked through: a device code sign-in approved by a user, illicit consent to a broad-scope application as persistence that survives password resets, and federated role assumption into cloud accounts through overly wide trust policies. All runs used synthetic identities in a mocked environment. The pre-generated lab output showed early identity steps at the blind level, with stronger coverage only where ownership was mature.

The takeaway is to build a coverage heat map, fix the weakest entry and exit points first, such as phishing-resistant MFA, token protection and device code restrictions, and then rerun the playbooks to confirm the scores improve. The speakers said the open-source tool and demo would be shared after the session.

talks.title: Field Notes on Offensive Agents - Reusability, Reliability
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from building reusable, reliable offensive AI agents for client web application tests, covering evaluation and safety controls.
talks.summary:
The speakers, from a security consultancy, start with the gap between flashy offensive agent demos and systems that can be trusted on client engagements. Their framework runs in four stages: discovery and reconnaissance, planning of vulnerability hypotheses, attack by specialised agents, and validation. Models are pluggable so different agents can use different models, and shared tools such as a browser can be reused across agents. A human still reviews findings before anything reaches a client report.

For reusability, they recommend turning a prompt that works for one vulnerability class into a template, sharing tooling instead of duplicating it, and packaging single agents so consultants can use them in their own harnesses. For reliability, structured output makes final reports easy to parse, validators cut false positives, and retries with backoff stop long runs from crashing when an API or tool fails. Authentication was the hardest problem, so they moved login flows into a dedicated subsystem that tracks sessions, cookies and keys.

On evaluation, they argue teams must define what success means, choose deterministic measures where possible, and decide what pass rate justifies release. They tested against internal labs, then bug bounty targets, to judge new models and prompt changes. Safety measures include an ask-human tool, a proxy that blocks out-of-scope hosts, careful wording in agent setup, and a kill switch. Their takeaway is that agents work best as a force multiplier running alongside human testers.

talks.title: Haetae - An Agent to Takedown N.Korean C2 Servers
talks.teaser: Shows how an AI agent built on Ruby and simple HTTP tools finds and exploits weak North Korean malware C2 servers, with an emulator for safe practice.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Haetae, an agent that profiles North Korean malware command-and-control infrastructure and exploits its weaknesses. The speakers, from a Web3 threat research team, triage three samples. A Go variant of GhostRAT has a second upload endpoint that skips the authentication required on the first. PowerfulArmadillo uses a proof-of-work step whose solved token is accepted indefinitely. MachoMan, a Go-based macOS sample, trusts any request that carries the expected user-agent string.

The exploits were first crafted by hand and then taught to an agent written in Ruby. It has four tools: GET, POST, PUT, and a proof-of-work solver. The proof of work was weak enough to solve on an ordinary phone. The agent works from a strict playbook that maps only known actions, and its prompts are written as if briefing a junior malware reverser. A companion emulator reproduces the minimal vulnerable endpoints, with per-family notes. Live demos showed the agent identifying a strain, solving the challenge, and uploading a file.

The speakers argue that flooding these servers with fake victims and fake data forces operators to spend time sorting noise or to fix their code, and they say the operators have not patched the flaws. The experiment cost under 70 cents in API spend. They also stress that researchers should understand a flaw manually before automating it. The Haetae code and the emulator were to be published on GitHub.

talks.title: From threat intel to tested defense the adversary simulation playbook
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how to turn threat intelligence into adversary simulation exercises that test whether detections and controls actually hold up.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by separating adversary simulation from emulation. Simulation means replaying real adversary behavior while adapting it to a specific environment and its existing controls. Emulation covers a wider scope. The panelists agree that red teams should still be free to push hard, and that threat intelligence should set priorities rather than dictate every command. Common mistakes they raised include copying breach-report indicators such as file hashes and command lines, relying on stale or incomplete reporting, and keeping red and blue teams apart.

In the middle section, they describe how to choose an actor: threat modeling by sector, geography and company size, and focusing on techniques peers are seeing, such as help-desk social engineering used against MFA. Their advice is to test the behavior behind a technique rather than one command line, so controls still work when an attacker changes details. Before running a full red team, they suggest building basics first, including asset inventory and purple-team tests of common techniques. Mature programs can make grading stricter, check network-layer coverage, and review whether alerts reach an actual response workflow.

The closing part covers low-budget options. Free resources such as Atomic Red Team and MITRE ATT&CK-based test plans let small teams start without paid intelligence. The panel also encouraged sharing knowledge and offering free seats at smaller events. The audience question on tabletop exercises ended with advice to include cross-functional staff and leadership, and to pre-test scenarios with technical staff.

talks.title: Hey Adversary, I’ve Got a Human EDR Bypass for You
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams read security awareness metrics, OSINT and employee habits to gain initial access without advanced code, and how defenders can respond.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a warning about compliance dashboards. A low phishing click rate can convince leadership that staff are secure, but the speaker argues that repetitive, template-based training teaches people a fixed set of warning signs. An attacker who learns those signs can build lures that leave them out, treating the trained human reaction as a predictable control to work around.

The middle section covers reconnaissance and pretexting. In a grey-box engagement, a client can share its awareness vendor, campaign cadence and test difficulty, and public professional posts can hint at which product and version a company runs. People also carry habits from earlier jobs, so a pretext that mirrors a former employer's ticketing or HR messages may succeed during the onboarding window. The speaker describes isolating a target outside the office in a restricted area, where staff feel protected, using a cheap drone drop. A short bonus segment covers physically taking a laptop whose BitLocker setup lacks a pre-boot PIN, with a claim that bus sniffing could expose the key.

The closing argument is that awareness programs should act as behavioral sensors rather than multiple-choice exams. Practical measures include interrupt protocols that break an attacker's live pace and a no-fault reporting culture meant to shorten dwell time.

talks.title: Microsoft and Amazon are my Favorite C2 Providers
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft Azure Relay and AWS IoT services can carry command-and-control traffic that blends into trusted cloud endpoints.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that managed cloud relay services from Microsoft and AWS make practical command-and-control channels. The speaker says many enterprises cannot block domains such as servicebus.windows.net or IoT endpoints without disrupting business tools that depend on them. In his framing, an attacker needs only code execution on a host and outbound HTTPS to reach the internet.

The talk covers three services. Azure Relay Bridge, a Microsoft open-source tool, tunnels TCP traffic through Azure's relay and can run as a persistent service. AWS IoT Secure Tunneling uses a localproxy binary, but sessions expire after 12 hours and bandwidth is capped. The speaker presents AWS IoT Core MQTT with X.509 mutual TLS as a longer-lived channel that avoids those limits. He also describes a red team test in which Azure Relay moved about a terabyte in roughly a day, and notes that the local endpoint traffic can look like a connection to localhost.

The closing section promises released Mythic agent profiles and detection guidance. Defenders should review CloudTrail and Entra ID activity for relay services and learn how these platforms behave before treating their traffic as routine.

talks.title: MCPwned - How Exposed AI Agents Became the Internet’s New Recon Toy
talks.teaser: Shows how internet scanners and attackers target exposed LLM gateways, MCP servers and local inference APIs, based on a multi-persona AI honeypot.
talks.summary:
Eli Woodward starts from a simple observation: scanning traffic on the public internet has shifted toward AI services. Cheap cloud instances logging web ports began showing requests for model lists and chat completions, so he built a honeypot that imitates many AI stacks across multiple ports and regions, capturing paths, headers, model names, prompts and the API keys that visitors try.

In a 48-hour window the sensors logged nearly four thousand requests from a few hundred source addresses, including MCP probes and many attempts with leaked or default keys. Woodward walks through one LiteLLM gateway compromise. The attacker used a default master key, listed existing models, registered new ones that pointed at an attacker-controlled host so traffic would be relayed there, and checked the setup with a single-character prompt. He also describes MCP enumeration aimed at tool lists, resource files and local database endpoints, and a relay service that appeared to resell access to exposed model servers.

His conclusion is that most of the abuse is basic misconfiguration rather than prompt injection, and that Docker hosts and laptops running local inference servers are targets too. The practical takeaways are to rotate default keys, log and restrict MCP resource reads, close default inference ports, and treat AI gateways as production infrastructure that needs monitoring and hardening guidance.

talks.title: SEND - Teaching Machines to Lie to Defenders
talks.teaser: Presents SEND, a framework that pairs cheap attacker actions with LLM-generated fake artifacts to mislead SOC analysts' investigation narratives.
talks.summary:
Deception research has long used decoy files and honeypots to catch attackers. This talk argues that SOC analysts instead build causal stories from related events, and that heuristics drive their attention: escalating high-severity alerts, end-of-chain activity such as staged encryption or exfiltration, and activity near domain controllers or executive endpoints. The speakers present SEND, a self-evolving framework that aims to corrupt the story defenders reconstruct during response rather than evade detection.

SEND combines low-cost actions with implanted artifacts. Failed credential-dumping reads, dummy outbound transfers of random bytes, and mass-created ransomware-style extensions produce real telemetry without needing to succeed. An LLM-driven narrative engine keeps emails, file logs and chat entries consistent with one false explanation, and a metric called INDR scores how far the defender's reconstruction diverges from the truth. The live demo was a scripted simulation, not an attack run. In a lab with Sysmon, Zeek and Splunk, an AI blue-team agent was increasingly misled as deception tiers were added. In a small study with four volunteer analysts, two reached the wrong attribution, and end-of-chain actions accounted for most of the misdirection.

The main takeaway is that detection was never the attack surface; investigation is. For defenders, this suggests checking whether reports weigh alternative explanations, not just whether an alert fired. The speakers' next steps are multi-agent pipelines where scenario generation and detection learn from each other.

talks.title: Where hackers find their people, and security finds its strength
talks.teaser: A panel of DEF CON organizers and community leaders shares how mentorship, welcoming villages and local meetups help newcomers find their place in security.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the panelists describing how they first got involved in hacker culture. One co-founded a conference and a local security group after attending DEF CON early on. Another created an arcade party that later moved under a veterans' association. A third came in from event logistics and ended up running live hacking events, and a fourth, a veteran, leads safety operations for a B-Sides conference. Each describes a moment when someone took them in and answered basic questions.

The middle of the discussion focuses on why people matter as much as tools. The panelists argue that people from different backgrounds solve problems differently, so a varied group produces better results. They describe hardware hackers who insisted on working together, teaching one another, and admitting what they did not know. They also cover a cyber activity book for children, built with a federal grant, which uses animals to teach passwords and cyberbullying. Several speakers say the community gave them a sense of belonging, leadership experience and lasting friendships, and one says it helped her through a hard transition out of the military.

The closing advice is practical. Newcomers should explore the different villages and interest groups rather than assume they must fit one track, start with local communities, and not worry about seeming unqualified. The takeaway is that welcoming, mentoring spaces are a real defensive asset, because they keep skilled people engaged and bring them into the field.

talks.title: Yet Another Walking Dead of Active Directory
talks.teaser: Shows how disabled and deleted Active Directory objects keep dangerous permissions and recoverable data, with open-source tools to find and abuse them.
talks.summary:
The talk is a follow-up to earlier research on disabled Active Directory accounts, which are often treated as harmless. The speaker shows that disabled users, computers and service accounts can keep dangerous inbound permissions, letting a low-privileged user reach domain admin through hidden ACL, group and delegation paths that BloodHound may not reveal. A real-world inspired case study anchors the walkthrough.

The second half turns to deleted objects and the Active Directory Recycle Bin. Deleted objects keep most of their attributes, so the speaker argues they matter most after domain admin is already gained, for persistence and pivoting, though they can enable lateral movement too. Recoverable leftovers include passwords stored in descriptions, orphaned SIDs still granted share access, SID history, and deleted group managed service accounts. The Python tool Necromancy checks whether the feature is on, restores objects, and calculates gMSA hashes offline once the KDS root key is known. Cobalt Strike object files cover the same checks.

The talk closes with defensive guidance. Disabled and deleted objects should be inventoried along with their inbound rights, and the speaker recommends treating the recycle bin as a place where secrets can survive. The Windows event IDs that record enabling accounts and changes to deleted objects are off by default, so auditing has to be switched on before an EDR can see them. A Sigma rule for these events is published alongside the tools.
